extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and judges (practitioners of patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and procedural rules governing the surrender of an original U.S. patent and the application, oath, scope, and effects of a re-issued patent (with historical statutory context, e.g., acts of 1870 and 1886).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender takes effect upon grant of re-issued patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of July 8, 1870, the surrender shall take effect upon the issue of the amended (re-issued) patent; until the re-issue is awarded the rights of the surrenderors are protected by the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to 1870 surrender was treated differently and could extinguish rights immediately; after 1870 the original remains in force until a re-issue is granted and, if the re-issue is refused, the original is returned to its owners. This rule protects holders during the re-issue process and fixes the time when surrender becomes effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: No valid surrender unless all owners concur
rubrics_metrics.description: A surrender cannot be valid and effective unless made with the concurrence of all the owners of the original patent (patentee, his representatives if he is dead and had not assigned the entire patent, and assignees of any undivided interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrence may be manifested by joining in the surrender or by subsequent ratification; under present Patent Office practice written consent of all owners must appear on the face of the reissue application. Grantees and licensees are not treated as owners whose concurrence is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender/re-issue must be made by appropriate party
rubrics_metrics.description: A surrender for re-issue must be made either by the patentee or by his representatives or assigns; where the whole interest has been assigned the surrender should be made by the assignee or with his consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignment of part of a patent does not entitle the assignee to surrender only that part; an assignee of an undivided interest must join. Surrender by a person other than the owner does not affect the owner's title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application for re-issue requires inventor's concurrence if living
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents granted or assigned since July 8, 1870, a re-issue can be granted only upon the application and oath of the original inventor, if he be living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legislative change requires the inventor's oath where the inventor is alive; when the inventor is dead the owners (representatives or assignees) may apply. The inventor's consent protects his interests (e.g., in future extensions or dependent inventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath must aver error arose from inadvertence, accident, or mistake and repeat original oath allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath accompanying a re-issue application must aver that the error whose amendment is desired arose through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and must repeat the allegations of the original oath regarding priority of invention and absence of prior public use and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This oath is prima facie evidence on the points embraced; it cannot be made by a mere assignee (if inventor is living) because inventor's positive knowledge is preferred over assignee's information and belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application must show original was defective and point out the mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for a re-issue must be based upon a single original patent and must show the original to have been defective through mistake, pointing out wherein the mistake consisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application comprises a petition (praying leave to surrender and for re-issue), an oath, an abstract of title, and the amended specification with necessary drawings/models. The application need not strictly follow statutory language but must disclose the defect and the single patent being amended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract of title and documentary evidence required with application
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract of title must disclose the names of all persons owning any undivided interest in the original patent; the original patent or, if lost, a certified copy with an affidavit of loss must be delivered to the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office practice requires proof of consent of assignees/owners, and a certified abstract of title is proper evidence of assignee's consent. These materials substantiate the application's legitimacy and chain of title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may be granted to assignees of any degree
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issued patent may be granted to assignees of any degree, however remote from the original inventor; the limits on amending description and claims are the same as if the inventor applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant of a re-issue to an assignee is prima facie evidence of his title. A re-issue obtained by an assignee enures to assignees by ratification, not by mere enurement if issued in patentee's name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue void if fraud is perpetrated or attempted
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue is void if any fraud is perpetrated or attempted by the applicant, for example where he knows that the original assignor was not the true inventor or that the alleged error did not occur in the manner asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fraud on the Patent Office or in the oath invalidates the re-issue. Courts scrutinize actual knowledge of falsity or intentional misrepresentation in the application process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender admits the original was inoperative/defective but not that it never existed
rubrics_metrics.description: Surrender of a patent for re-issue is an admission that the original patent is defective (inoperative), and the Commissioner's acceptance is a judgment that amendment by re-issue is required; it is not a concession that the original never existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects: closed transactions under the original remain undisturbed; judgments obtained on the original are not vacated; moneys paid under it cannot be reclaimed. However, suits based on infringement under the original cannot be maintained after surrender; actions can be brought on the re-issue for infringements continuing after its grant, with damages accruing since the date of the re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue is a continuation of the original and governed by same law
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issued patent is a new statement (continuation) of the contract between the public and the patentee and is to be interpreted by the same rules as an original patent; rights arising under it are governed by the law in force when the original was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability of what is claimed in the re-issue is determined by the state of the art as of the original application's date. The motive for obtaining a re-issue is generally unimportant unless there is actual fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot affect rights of non-consenting owners or third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: No re-issue of a patent can affect the rights of non-consenting owners or other third parties; parties claiming under the original patent may retain existing rights or assert them as modified by the re-issue at their option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-consenting assignees may repudiate the re-issue and insist upon privileges under the original; grantees/licensees retain local or individual rights until they voluntarily relinquish them and accept rights under the re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor cannot unilaterally apply to re-issue an assigned patent without assignee consent
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor has no authority to apply for the re-issue of an assigned patent without the consent of his assignees; such a wrongful application cannot impair assignees' rights, and they may ratify or repudiate the re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor refuses to apply for re-issue when necessary, he may be compelled by a court of equity to do so. Proof of assignee consent (e.g., abstract of title) is required in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition signatures and consent formalities vary with grant/assignment date
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition for re-issue must be signed by the true owners of the patent unless the patent was granted or transferred since July 8, 1870, in which case the petition must be signed by the inventor if living and contain the written assent of the present owners; if the inventor is dead and petition bears assignees' signatures, the fact of his decease must be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signature and assent formalities reflect statutory changes; failure to follow proper signature/assent requirements can affect validity or processing of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application must be based on a single original patent (not multiple patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue can be based only upon a single original patent and not upon several originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple earlier patents are implicated, separate proceedings/applications are necessary; the re-issue application must identify the single patent being amended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on amendment of description and claims same as if inventor applied
rubrics_metrics.description: The limits within which the original description and claims may be amended in a re-issue, and the consequences of prior disclaimer or abandonment, are the same as if the application had been made by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments cannot exceed the permissible scope (as determined by law and the original disclosure); previous disclaimers or abandonments affect what may properly be reclaimed or broadened in the re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may be used to secure rights for different territorial portions of the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: A portion or the whole of an invention for a particular part of the United States, and the rest for other portions, may be secured by a re-issue (e.g., separate patents covering separate parts may together constitute one effective patenting scheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two patents for separate parts may, in effect, constitute but one patent for the whole invention; but re-issues cannot expand the lawful monopoly beyond what is authorized by law.
